passage: In Rania's class in Madrid, a boy announced that kids who drink energy drinks score better in football trials, because "all the best players on the team drink them." Javier nodded along. Rania didn't. At lunch she said, "Maybe the best players just train more and buy drinks with their pocket money. The drink isn't the reason." Javier looked annoyed. "The coach even said they help." "Did he show anything? Or just say it?" Rania asked. That evening Javier searched for proper studies and found none that tested it. He grudgingly texted her: "Ok, no proof 🙄 still tasty." Rania sent back a thumbs-up and a note to check with the coach about the claim.

qa.q: What did the boy claim about energy drinks?
qa.a: He claimed that kids who drink them score better in football trials because all the best players drink them.

qa.q: How can you tell Javier was reluctant to change his mind?
qa.a: He looked annoyed and pointed to the coach, and even his text admitting there was no proof sounded grudging.

qa.q: What did Rania do that others could copy when they hear a claim?
qa.a: She asked whether something else could explain the pattern and whether the coach showed evidence or only said it.

qa.q: How might the boy who made the claim feel if Rania questioned him in class?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed or defensive, so a calm question in private may have gone down better than calling him out.

grounding: It shows teens questioning a claim that confuses correlation with causation and relies on authority rather than evidence.

passage: In the physics lab, Swati's group had to test whether heavier balls roll down the ramp faster. Aparna, the topper, said, "Of course they do, my brother said so." Swati wasn't so sure. "Let's just time it." They rolled a steel ball and a marble five times each. The results were almost the same, and the small differences kept changing. Aparna frowned at the notebook. "Maybe we did it wrong." Swati suggested they try ten more times, and change who held the stopwatch. The results still matched. Aparna crossed out her prediction and wrote the real numbers. "My brother's going to argue," she said. Swati grinned. "Show him the notebook."

qa.q: How many times did they roll each ball at first?
qa.a: They rolled each ball five times.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling when she frowned at the notebook?
qa.a: She was uneasy and a bit reluctant, because the results went against what she had been sure of and what her brother had said.

qa.q: Why was repeating the test and changing the stopwatch holder a good idea?
qa.a: It checked whether the result was due to chance or one person's timing, so the conclusion rested on stronger evidence.

qa.q: How might Aparna's brother react to the notebook?
qa.a: He might argue at first, but the repeated measurements give Aparna evidence that is harder to dismiss than just his opinion.

grounding: It shows teens judging a claim by testing it rather than trusting who said it.

passage:
Dear Chinmay,
You forwarded me that message again, the one saying people who eat breakfast early live longer, "backed by doctors." I know you mean well. But I read the actual study. They only found early eaters tend to live longer. It didn't prove breakfast does it. Maybe early eaters sleep earlier, walk more, or just have calmer jobs. And "backed by doctors" didn't name a single doctor.
I'm not saying breakfast is bad. Eat it if you like it! I'm saying the message sounds more sure than the study is. If you're worried about health, ask your own doctor.
Also please stop forwarding stuff to the family group at 6 am. Nani's phone buzzes and wakes her up 😅
Your brother,
Omkar

qa.q: What did the forwarded message claim?
qa.a: It claimed people who eat breakfast early live longer and said it was backed by doctors.

qa.q: What does Omkar's line "I know you mean well" show about his feelings?
qa.a: He wants to correct Chinmay without hurting him, showing care for his brother even while disagreeing.

qa.q: What made Omkar's reply to the message sensible?
qa.a: He read the actual study, pointed out other explanations, noticed no doctor was named, and suggested asking a real doctor instead of trusting forwards.

qa.q: If you were Chinmay, how might you feel reading this email?
qa.a: You might feel a little corrected, but the warm tone and the joke about Nani's phone would make it easier to accept. 🙂

grounding: A teen's email to his brother separates correlation from causation and questions a claim resting on vague authority.

passage: So Suraj, you know Rakesh sir, the one who's always on those study videos? He said students who study with music score higher. Everyone in our class started repeating it. Even my cousin put on headphones while doing trigonometry. I got curious and found the survey he quoted. It was twenty students from one coaching centre. Twenty! And they just asked them if they liked music and what their marks were. It didn't test anything. Maybe kids who can afford their own quiet room with speakers also have tutors. That's correlation, not causation, right? I'm not saying music is bad. I'm saying a famous person repeating something ten times doesn't make it evidence. Now I ask: how big was the study, and what did they actually measure?

qa.q: How many students were in the survey Rakesh sir quoted?
qa.a: Twenty students from one coaching centre.

qa.q: What made the narrator curious enough to look up the survey?
qa.a: Everyone was repeating the claim, even the narrator's cousin, and the narrator wanted to know if it was really true.

qa.q: What questions does the narrator now use to judge a claim?
qa.a: How big the study was and what it actually measured, rather than trusting who said it.

qa.q: How might the narrator's classmates react to these findings?
qa.a: Some might feel silly for copying the idea, while others might defend the famous teacher out of habit.

grounding: A teen explains judging a claim by the quality of evidence and spotting correlation versus causation, not authority.

passage: I'm Ganga, Tushar's older sister. For the science fair, he wanted to test whether plants grow better with music, because his friend's uncle swore by it and everyone in the building repeated it. First he put a pot beside the radio on the sunny windowsill and another in the corner. The windowsill plant grew taller. He was thrilled. Then he stopped and stared at them for ages. I don't know what went through his head. The next day he moved both plants to the same windowsill, same water, same soil, and played music to only one. Three weeks later they were almost the same height. He wrote on his chart: 'Sunlight, not songs?' His teacher gave him a special mention.

qa.q: Where did Tushar first place the plant with the radio?
qa.a: On the sunny windowsill.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt as he stared at the plants for ages?
qa.a: He may have gone from thrilled to doubtful, noticing the windowsill plant also had more sunlight, though Ganga isn't sure.

qa.q: Why was Tushar's second experiment better than the first?
qa.a: He kept sunlight, water and soil the same so only the music differed, which gave fairer evidence.

qa.q: How might the friend's uncle respond to Tushar's result?
qa.a: He might be surprised or unwilling to believe it, since he had repeated the claim with such confidence.

grounding: An observer describes a teen testing a repeated claim and separating correlation from cause.
